concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by contrast signal and synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. In film studies—a visually oriented discipline that is ______ backlit close-ups, eyeline matches, and voyeuristic gazes—scholars have often been tone-deaf to the sounds of music. Choices: (A) fixated on, (B) obsessed with, (C) unconcerned with, (D) amused by, (E) bothered by, (F) indifferent to.

solution.operation: Read the sentence as a contrast between the discipline's treatment of the visual and its treatment of the aural ("tone-deaf to the sounds of music").
solution.result: The visual is attended to; the aural is relatively ignored in favor of it.
solution.description: Establish the sentence's internal opposition first: the second half says scholars ignore sound, so the first half must say what they do attend to. This fixes the direction the blank has to point.

solution.operation: Require the blank to designate attention to the visual elements listed (backlit close-ups, eyeline matches, voyeuristic gazes).
solution.result: The blank must express strong attention, not lack of it.
solution.description: Convert the contrast into a concrete requirement on the missing word, so each option can be tested against a single criterion rather than judged by feel.

solution.operation: Eliminate "unconcerned with" (C) and "indifferent to" (F) because they do not designate attention.
solution.result: C and F are out.
solution.description: Drop the choices that fail the attention criterion outright — they describe the discipline's stance toward music, not toward the visual.

solution.operation: Test "amused by" (D): compare its degree of attention and its affect against "fixated on" and "obsessed with," and look for a second choice that would give it the same meaning.
solution.result: "Amused by" conveys a lesser degree of attention and a more positive affect, and has no partner word among the choices.
solution.description: Because the answer must be a pair producing sentences alike in meaning, a word with no equivalent partner is eliminated even before its fit is judged; "amused by" also understates the attention required in step 2.

solution.operation: Pair the two remaining attention words, "fixated on" (A) and "obsessed with" (B).
solution.result: Choice A and Choice B both satisfy the blank and produce sentences alike in meaning.
solution.description: Confirm the surviving two are synonymous in this context, which is what a Sentence Equivalence answer requires — both fit and both yield the same completed sentence.

examples.answer: Choice A: fixated on AND Choice B: obsessed with

key_reminders: A Sentence Equivalence answer is a pair: a word that fits alone but has no synonymous partner among the choices cannot be correct.
A contrast cue elsewhere in the sentence (here, "tone-deaf to the sounds of music") fixes the direction the blank must take.
Match degree and affect, not just topic — a milder or more positive word can fit loosely and still be wrong.
common_mistakes: Picking "unconcerned with" or "indifferent to" by carrying over the sentence's "tone-deaf" idea to the wrong half of the contrast.
Choosing "amused by" because it plausibly describes a viewer's response, ignoring that it has no synonymous partner among the six choices.

concept.technique_name: explain the discrepancy (EXCEPT) via the 4-step Critical Reasoning process
concept.sub_category: Critical Reasoning — Evidence Family / Explain the Discrepancy

examples.problem_statement: Hunting Season. In an effort to reduce the number of deer, and therefore decrease the number of automobile accidents caused by deer, the government lengthened the deer hunting season earlier this year. Surprisingly, the number of accidents caused by deer has increased substantially since the introduction of the longer hunting season. All of the following, if true, help to explain the increase in traffic accidents caused by deer EXCEPT (A) The presence of humans in the woods causes the deer to move to new areas, which causes the deer to cross roads more frequently than normal. (B) In the area where the deer live, the lengthened hunting season attracted a significantly greater amount of traffic than usual this year. (C) Most automobile accidents involving deer result from cars swerving to avoid deer, and they leave the deer in question unharmed. (D) Deer tend to bolt when hearing gunshots or other loud sounds and are more likely to run across a road without warning. (E) A new highway was recently built directly through the state's largest forest, which is the primary habitat of the state's deer population.

solution.operation: Identify the question: the phrase "help to explain" plus "EXCEPT" marks this as a Discrepancy EXCEPT question.
solution.result: Question type: Explain the Discrepancy, EXCEPT format.
solution.description: Read the question stem before the argument and classify it, because the type determines what the right answer must do — here the wording tells you four choices will resolve the puzzle and one will not.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument into its causal chain: longer hunting season → fewer deer → fewer car accidents.
solution.result: Government plan: increased hunting season leads to decreased deer, which leads to decreased car accidents.
solution.description: Map the intended multi-level chain on paper so the surprising outcome can be placed against a specific expectation rather than a vague impression.

solution.operation: Add the surprising evidence: accidents caused by deer have increased substantially since the longer season began.
solution.result: Observed outcome is the exact opposite of the predicted one — the discrepancy to be explained.
solution.description: State the contradiction explicitly, because every answer choice will be judged by whether it accounts for more accidents, not for accidents in general.

solution.operation: State the goal: find the one choice that does NOT explain why accidents increased; cross off the four that do.
solution.result: Right answer = the odd one out that fails to fix the discrepancy.
solution.description: Set the elimination rule before touching the choices, so the EXCEPT format does not invert your instinct to keep whatever sounds reasonable.

solution.operation: Test (A): longer season means people in the woods longer, so deer cross roads more frequently than they otherwise would.
solution.result: Increases the likelihood of deer-caused accidents — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Check whether the choice supplies a mechanism that raises the accident count, and eliminate it when it does, since explaining choices are the wrong answers here.

solution.operation: Test (B): the lengthened season attracted significantly more traffic than usual to the area where the deer live.
solution.result: More cars where the deer are means more chances for collisions — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Note that this choice raises accidents through the other side of the collision (cars, not deer), which still resolves the puzzle, so it is eliminated.

solution.operation: Test (C): most deer-related accidents come from cars swerving to avoid deer, leaving the deer unharmed.
solution.result: Explains how accidents happen but says nothing about the number of accidents rising — does not resolve the discrepancy.
solution.description: Separate mechanism from magnitude: this choice describes the form accidents take, and because the discrepancy is about an increase in count, it is the one that fails and therefore the answer.

solution.operation: Test (D): deer bolt at gunshots and are more likely to run across a road without warning.
solution.result: A longer season means more gunshots over more time, so more sudden crossings — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Confirm the choice ties the change (a longer season) to more accident opportunities, which disqualifies it in an EXCEPT question.

solution.operation: Test (E): a new highway was built directly through the forest that is the deer's primary habitat.
solution.result: The situation changed from the prior year in a way that would raise deer-caused accidents — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Accept an alternative cause as an explanation — a Discrepancy answer need not involve the hunting season at all, only account for the rise — leaving (C) as the sole non-explainer.

key_reminders: On a Discrepancy EXCEPT question the four choices that resolve the puzzle are the wrong answers; the one that fails to resolve it is correct.
The discrepancy here is about the number of accidents increasing, so a choice must bear on quantity, not merely on how accidents occur.
An answer may explain the rise through an unrelated cause (a new highway) and still count as explaining.
common_mistakes: Reversing the EXCEPT format and selecting (A) or (D) because they explain the increase well.
Accepting (C) as an explanation because it describes deer accidents plausibly, without asking whether it shows the count going up.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion driven by a contrast connective

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Researchers trying to make it possible to trace counterfeit documents to the printer that produced them are (i) ______ the fact that the rotating drums and mirrors inside laser printers are imperfect devices that leave unique patterns of banding in their output. Although these patterns are (ii) ______ to the naked eye, they can be (iii) ______ and analyzed by computer programs that the researchers have spent the past year devising. Blank (i): A exploiting, B facing, C manipulating. Blank (ii): D invisible, E obvious, F unappealing. Blank (iii): G detected, H implemented, I generated.

solution.operation: Note the "although" that begins the second sentence and read it as a contrast between how the naked eye perceives the patterns and how computer programs view them.
solution.result: Blanks (ii) and (iii) must stand in opposition to each other.
solution.description: Start with the connective, since it is the only explicit logical signal in the passage and it links the two blanks in the same sentence — solving them as a pair is easier than solving either alone.

solution.operation: Search the columns for the (ii)/(iii) pairing that produces that eye-versus-computer contrast: invisible/obvious/unappealing against detected/implemented/generated.
solution.result: "Invisible" and "detected" are the only pairing that creates the contrast.
solution.description: Test the pairs jointly rather than the words separately; the eye fails to see the patterns while the programs pick them out, which only invisible-plus-detected expresses.

solution.operation: Characterize what Blank (i) must express: the relationship between the researchers and the inevitability of imperfections in printing technology.
solution.result: The blank names how the researchers treat an unavoidable flaw.
solution.description: Define the job of the remaining blank before scanning its column, so the choice is judged against the passage's logic instead of against which word sounds most sophisticated.

solution.operation: Apply the passage's assertion that the researchers use computers to analyze these imperfections to the Blank (i) column.
solution.result: "Exploiting" is the best choice, since the researchers turn the flaw to their advantage.
solution.description: Use the information already established in step 2 — the programs detect and analyze the banding — as the evidence that selects the first blank, which is why the blanks are solved out of order.

solution.operation: Rule out the other Blank (i) options: weigh "facing" and "manipulating" against that same assertion.
solution.result: "Facing" does not imply the level of engagement detailed in the passage; "manipulating" suggests changing the imperfections rather than analyzing them.
solution.description: Confirm the pick by naming the specific defect in each rival — too little engagement in one case, the wrong kind of action in the other — rather than dismissing them by feel.

examples.answer: Choice A: exploiting; Choice D: invisible; Choice G: detected

key_reminders: "Although" signals contrast: the two blanks it joins must oppose each other.
Solve the blank with the strongest textual signal first, then use what it establishes to fix the remaining blank — order of blanks need not be order of solving.
A wrong choice can fail on degree of engagement ("facing") or on direction of action ("manipulating"), not only on topic.
common_mistakes: Choosing "manipulating" for Blank (i) because researchers are working with the printer flaws, when the passage has them analyzing rather than altering those flaws.
Filling Blank (ii) with "obvious" and Blank (iii) with "detected," which destroys the contrast "although" demands.

concept.technique_name: solving a reciprocal-sum rational equation by splitting the right side into reciprocal fractions

examples.problem_statement: Using the Equation Solving with Reciprocals technique, work two algebraic equations: first a linear equation admitting two possible interpretations, then the rational equation \frac{x}{x+1} + \frac{x+1}{x} = \frac{169}{60}. Given the factor pairs of 60 (2 \times 30, 3 \times 20, 4 \times 15, 5 \times 12, 6 \times 10), the matching pair 5 and 12 with 5^2 + 12^2 = 169, and the decomposition \frac{169}{60} = \frac{12}{5} + \frac{5}{12}. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: x+2 = 4 \text{ or } x+2 = 1, \text{ denominator } x+3 \text{ in both cases}
solution.result: Two readings of the first equation: \frac{4}{x+3} = \frac{x+2}{1}\text{-style and its counterpart}
solution.description: Record that the printed first equation is ambiguous and admits two interpretations, both sharing the denominator x+3; each reading has to be carried through separately.

solution.operation: 4(x+3) = x+2 \quad \text{and} \quad 4(x+2) = x+3
solution.result: Two cross-multiplied linear equations
solution.description: Cross-multiply each interpretation to clear the fraction, turning both readings into plain linear equations.

solution.operation: 4x+12 = x+2 \quad \text{and} \quad 4x+8 = x+3
solution.result: Both sides expanded
solution.description: Distribute the 4 across each bracket so that the x-terms and constants stand separately and can be collected.

solution.operation: 4x-x = 2-12 \quad \text{and} \quad 4x-x = 3-8
solution.result: x-terms on the left, constants on the right
solution.description: Rearrange each equation, moving the x-terms to one side and the constants to the other.

solution.operation: 3x = -10 \quad \text{and} \quad 3x = -5
solution.result: x = -\frac{10}{3} \quad \text{and} \quad x = -\frac{5}{3}
solution.description: Combine like terms and divide by 3 to solve each interpretation, giving the two possible values for the first equation.

solution.result: The second equation, now to be solved
solution.description: Turn to the second problem and write out the rational equation that the reciprocal technique will handle.

solution.operation: \frac{x}{x+1} \text{ and } \frac{x+1}{x} \text{ are reciprocals}
solution.result: The left side is a sum of a fraction and its reciprocal
solution.description: Recognize the structural feature the whole method rests on: the two terms on the left invert each other, so the right side must decompose the same way.

solution.operation: 60 = 2 \times 30 = 3 \times 20 = 4 \times 15 = 5 \times 12 = 6 \times 10
solution.result: All factor pairs of the denominator 60
solution.description: Factorize the denominator 60 into every pair of factors, since a reciprocal split \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} has denominator ab.

solution.result: The pair 5 and 12 matches the numerator 169
solution.description: Test the factor pairs to find the one whose squares add to the numerator 169, because \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}.

solution.result: Right side written as a sum of reciprocal fractions
solution.description: Rewrite the right-hand side using the matched pair, so both sides of the equation now have the identical reciprocal-sum form.

solution.operation: \frac{x}{x+1} = \frac{12}{5} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{x+1}{x} = \frac{5}{12} \quad \text{(or vice versa)}
solution.result: Two simple proportions replacing the rational equation
solution.description: Match the terms on the left to the terms on the right term by term; either assignment is admissible, which is why the technique yields corresponding pairs of values.

solution.operation: \text{Solve either proportion for } x
solution.result: The corresponding values of x
solution.description: Cross-multiply whichever proportion you prefer and solve it for x — the book stops here, leaving the final arithmetic to the reader.

examples.answer: First equation has two possible solutions: x = -10/3 or x = -5/3. Second equation can be solved by equating x/(x+1)=12/5 or 5/12, giving corresponding x values.

key_reminders: \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}: the denominator of the sum is the product of the pair and the numerator is the sum of their squares.
To split a target fraction into reciprocals, list the factor pairs of its denominator and test which pair's squares add to its numerator.
Once both sides are reciprocal sums, the terms can be equated pairwise, and either assignment is valid.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the first factor pair of 60 instead of testing pairs until 5^2 + 12^2 = 169 is reached.
Equating only one way (\frac{x}{x+1} = \frac{12}{5}) and missing that the reversed assignment is equally admissible.
Solving only one interpretation of the ambiguous first equation and reporting a single value instead of both -\frac{10}{3} and -\frac{5}{3}.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion using an explicit contrast between time periods

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. In stark contrast to his later (i) ______ , Simpson was largely (ii) ______ politics during his college years, despite the fact that the campus he attended was rife with political activity. Blank (i): A activism, B apathy, C affability. Blank (ii): D devoted to, E indifferent to, F shaped by.

solution.operation: Read "In stark contrast to his later ..." as setting Simpson's college-year relation to politics against his later relation to politics.
solution.result: The two blanks must contrast with each other.
solution.description: Identify the contrast frame first, because it is what ties the two blanks together and means neither can be chosen in isolation.

solution.operation: Read the "despite" clause: the campus was rife with political activity, yet Simpson's college-year stance is being singled out.
solution.result: In college, Simpson did not engage with the political activity around him.
solution.description: Use the concessive clause to pin down Blank (ii)'s direction — "despite" only makes sense if his behavior ran against the surrounding activity, i.e., nonengagement.

solution.operation: Test the Blank (ii) column for that nonengagement: devoted to, indifferent to, shaped by.
solution.result: Only "indifferent to" conveys nonengagement.
solution.description: Match each option against the requirement established in step 2; "devoted to" and "shaped by" both describe engagement and so contradict the "despite" clause.

solution.operation: Test the Blank (i) column for the required contrast with "indifferent to": activism, apathy, affability.
solution.result: Only "activism" supplies the contrast.
solution.description: Now that Blank (ii) is settled, pick the later-life quality that opposes indifference — "apathy" would repeat it rather than contrast, and "affability" is off the political topic entirely.

examples.answer: Choice A: activism; Choice E: indifferent to

key_reminders: "In stark contrast" requires the two blanks to oppose each other, not merely to be plausible on their own.
A "despite" clause tells you the subject behaved against the surrounding circumstance — here, disengagement amid campus political activity.
Solve the blank the text constrains most tightly first, then use it to fix the other.
common_mistakes: Selecting "apathy" for Blank (i), which echoes rather than contrasts with the college-year indifference the sentence describes.
Selecting "shaped by" or "devoted to" for Blank (ii) by reading the campus's political activity as something Simpson took part in, which the "despite" clause rules out.
